summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965), in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting, the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The contention found favour with the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner and accordingly deleted the additions of Rs 1, 50,000 representing accrued interest. In doing so, the Appellate Tribunal followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth Tax officer appealed to this Court by way of reference under section 257 of the Income tax Act, 1961 for the opinion of this Court on the following question of law: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the wealth Tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee interest due on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lent business, the accounts of the respondent being maintained on cash basis ?" The High Court dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the reference to this court, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth tax Act wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net income of the assesee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate values of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation day. " According to the scheme of the wealth Act, the net Wealth Tax of an assessee has to be determined as it obtains on a particular date. That is the "valuation date".

Respondent in the appeal was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was incharge of preparing the pay bills and other bills of the work charg ed employees of the project. He made this entry with ulterior motive to withdraw the pay of Ashok Kumar for the month of May 1969 even though Ash ok Kumar was not working in that Division. A bogus identi ty card in the name of Ashok kumar T.No. 59 T with the sign a tures of the issuing officer was also prepared by the r e spondent although it was not his duty to prepare the ident i ty card. The said fictitious identity card was used by o ne Suraj Singh, cleaner T. No. 210 K of Beggi Tunnelling Divi sion for the purpose of withdrawing the pay. While Suraj Singh by impersonation was receiving the pay ment of Ashok Kuma r, he was recognised by the Cashier since he kn ew him personally. There then started an enquiry followed by departmental proceedings against three persons includ ing the respondent herein. The Personnel Officer of the 23 BSL Project was appointed as Inquiry Officer. He framed charge against the responde nt in the following terms: "That the said Shri Parma Nand, while working as Time Keeper, in time Keeping Sub Division of Beasput Li nk Project, Sundarnagar during the month May 1969 failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty in as mu ch he falsely marked the attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar Token N o. 59 at serial No. 10 on page 2 of the relevant pay roll. " The Inquiry Officer framed charges against the respondent in the above terms: That the said Sri Parma n Nand, While working as time Keeper in Time Keeping Sub division of Sundernagar during th month of June 1969 failed t hat he failed to maintaining absolute integrity & devotion to duties in as much as he falsely mark ed the attendance. An appreciation of the evidence, as done in the preceding pages, would sh ow that the applicant had entered the name o f Ashok Kumar in the pay roll for May 1969 and so far as other other eviden ce against him is concerned, it is mostly of a circumstanti al nature. There was no direct or expert evidence that it was he who had initiated t he identity card. It was ly contended on behalf of the appel lant that if the enquiry held against the delinquent offi cer was proper with the findings supported by evidence, the Tribunal cannot substitute its own judgment to mod i fy the punishment awarded. On the other hand, an order bas ed on several grounds some of which are found to be non existent or irrelevant, and there is nothing to show that the authori ty would have passed the order on t he basis of the other relevant and existing grounds, and t he exclusion of the irrelevant or non exist ent grounds cou ld not have affected the ultimate opinion or decision. In dismissing th at appeal, Shalat, J., made inter alia, the following observ a tions: "The findings in respect of charges l(a) and l(e) 29 should be set aside as being opposed to the rules of natur al justice, but the findings in regard of charge l(c) a nd l(d) need not be disturbed. It will be left to Government to decide whether, on the basis of t he charges, the punishment of dismissal should be maintain ed or else whether a lesser punishment would suffice." The Supreme Court reversed this order on the ground that it is not commensurate with t he delinquency of the official. The constitutional guarantee afforded to a publ ic servant is that he shall not be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed, a nd that he shah not be dismiss ed or reduced in ra nk until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showi ng against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him.

The appellants are the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit was for a mere declaration simpliciter could not lie. On the dismissal of the said suit, the original plaintiff filed another suit No. 114/74 on May 6, 1974 for restoration of possession on the grounds that he was the lawful tenant of the property and since he had not been dispossessed, in accordance with law, the defen dants who were mere trespassers were liable to be evicted therefrom. The Trial Court upheld the plaintiffs contention that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed, the second Suit was clearly barred by Order 2 rule 2(2)(3)of the Code. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. There can, therefore be no doubt that after the Fifth Amendment became effective in regard to land used primarily for growing coconut trees and garden produce, the jurisdiction of Civil Court was ousted by virtue of section 58(2) from settling decide, deciding and dealing with such question as : (i) Whether any person is a tenant or should be deemed to be a tenant under the Act, the Mamlatdar shall decide such question; (ii) Whether the tenancy of any deemed tenant is legally terminated and if no, whether the tenant evicted from the land held by him as such is entitled to restoration of Possession? The jurisdiction is, therefore vested in the Mamlatdar under Section 7 read with section 58 of the Act and section 58 (2), specifically bars the jurisdictionof all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any questions which is by or under the act required to he settled, decide, decided or dealt with; (iii) Whether a person is not a tenant in respect of the lands in question should be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil court if the issue is held against defendant No1, the Civil Judge may consider passing of a decree in eviction but if on the other hand he is held to be tenant, the civil Court may be required to dismiss the suit.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2 grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the Corpo ration). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. They want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They also seek regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion, gratuity etc. The Corporation resisted the petitioners ' claim and contended that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act, and as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. A little more information about the purpose and object of the Corpora tion would be useful for proper understanding of the case. The Corpora tation has been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. With these facts, the Court directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioners on par with his counterparts doing identical work under the same employer. In the immediate aftermath of the decision in Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; this Court in Randhir singh vs Union Of India, , has innovated that it is a constitu tional goal capable of being achieved through constitutional remedies. There the Court pointed out that principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is, therefore not impermissible to provide two different pay scales in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It was pointed out by this Court that in service, merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or sheearns also by experience as much as by other means. Apart from that, the court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Anr., ; , referred to.

Charge No. 1 framed in this case was for criminal conspiracy under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. on the allegation that between the first week of October 1975 and 2.1.1976 at Baburbara village, all the seven accused and the approver P.W. 1 entered into a criminal conspiracy to commit murders of young girls and women in the vicinity of Babulta village by giving injuries on their private parts or disfaviguring the faces in Order to make them appear that they committed three murder of Malan and Waghala villages by inflicting blows on the Private parts of victims or configuring its faces in orders to make It appear that Shivram, P.Ws. 45 saw accused 6 under a vad tree and Abasaheb, P P. Ws. 44, saw him in the rivulet; and (4) retracted judicial confession, Exh. 138 of accused 6. The High Court acquitted accused 2 to 4 and convicted accused 1 alone of that charge and sentenced him, holding that he and some others had conspired together and fabricated the deed of assignment put forward by accused 1 and that accused 1 only could not have fabricated that document. Allowing the appeals of accused No. 5 and 6, this Court, HELD: (1) The retracted judicial confessions of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5 had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge of conspiracy under Section 302 readwith section 120 B I.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, (exhibit A) in favour of her husband Sadagopalachar, died in July 1903 leaving behind him his adopted son, the appellant and two daughters Gundamma alias Ranganayakamma who is still alive and Lakshmma alias Achamma who is alleged to had executed the will in suit and died thereafter on September 26, 1945 at Mandya. Respondents 2 to 4 were the sons of the appellant. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against respondents 1 to 4 on the ground that the will propounded by him was not genuine or valid and that at the material time Lakshmamamma had a half share in all the properties comprised in the said deed of gift in favour Of her husband. The trial court held that the appellant had failed to prove that the money for the purchase of items 3, 4 and 5 came out of any bequest under Annaji 's will (ex exhibit A) and so in its opinion it was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmabai. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that even if it had found in favourof the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that he had entirely failed to establish that the amount for purchase of item 3,4 and 5 fell out of or any bequest thereunder. On the question whether the will set up by the propounder was proved to he last will of the testator has to be decided in the light of these provisions. Held: (i) It is true that if a caveat is filed alleging the exercise of undue influence, fraud or coercion in respect of the execution of the Will propounded, such pleas may have to be proved by the caveators; but even without such pleas circumstances may raise a doubt as to whether the testator was acting of his own free will in executing the will and in such circumstances it would be a part of the initial onus to remove any such legitimate doubts in the matter. If it is shown that the propounder has taken a prominent part in the execution, of the will, and has received substantial benefit under it, that itself is generally treated as a suspicious circumstance attending the execution by the testator and the propounder is required to remove the said suspicions from the mind of the court by cogent and satisfactory evidence.

The appellant company manufactured Arcons, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons", manufactured by the appellant company. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbons manufactured by it could be covered by the entry under consideration. It however held that such arc carbonons were covered by Entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the appeal without taking further evidence. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods under consideration are covered by Item No.4 of the first schedule to the Andhra pradesh General Sales tax Act, and therefore, they fall under Entry No., 4 of Schedule 1 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience or effectiveness of something else". Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance", "additional"; "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." "Accessories" are not necessarily confined to particular machines for which they; may serve as aids. The same item may be an accessory of more than one kind of instrument. It will be noticed that the entry shows that some precision has been attempted in making the entries. When it was intended to confine the entry to particular gadgets and "parts thereof" the entry said so. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for Use for a particular kind of instruments of gadget only, the article, manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of instrument would not cease to be covered under the intended Entry simply because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [564B C] 2. The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that the main use of the arc car bons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that the appellants are known as 'cinema are carboons in the market.

Section 15 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules, 1966 empowers the Central Government to enhance or reduce the rate of royalty prescribed by the Second Schedule in respect of any mineral subject to the condition that the Central Govern ment shall not enhance the rate Of royalty in respect thereof of any minor mineral more than once during any period of three years. Section 14 of the Act provides that sections 5 to 13 (inclusive) shall not apply to quarry leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor minerals and for purposes connected therewith. Clause (e) of the said section defines 'minor minerals ' as building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand other than sand used for prescribed purposes and any other mineral which the Central Govt may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be a minor mineral. It is not disputed that Black Trap and Hard Murrum are notified as minor minerals. The Act has made provision with regard to the issue of prospecting licences and mining leases in respect Of minor minerals which are won by the mining lease holders under the Act at the rates prescribed in the Second schedule to the Act. Under section 3A of the the Act the word 'minerals ' is defined as including all minerals except mineral oils. Clause 2(vi)(a) defines "minor minerals" as building stone stones, ravel, normal clay, sand other then sand used or for prescribed purpose and any further mineral which is the Central Gov ernment may, from time to time by notification, in the official Gazette, specify. Rule 21 of the Rules provides that a holder of a mining lease granted under the Rules shall pay royalty at the rate prescribed for the time being in the rules framed by the State Government in respect o f minor minerals provided in column 2 of the Schedule removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the scales specified against them in column 3 of the schedule. Rule 22 provides that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of village potters if their annual produc tion is not exceeding two lakh bricks and they supply at least one lakh bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. The validity of rule 21 as it existed prior to the issuance of the impugned notification was considered in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and Ors., [1989] 4 S.C.C., Judgments Today 190 that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the state, the levy was bad. The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of Rule 21 which was substituted in the place of the former rule 21 by a new rule which reads thus: "21. Rate of royalty in case of specified minor minerals has been enhanced from Rs.4 to Rs.7 per metric tonne. The contention of the petitioners was that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Govern ment had to be used only for minerals and could not be used for any other purpose. According to them the Act had been passed for purposes of regulation and development of minerals. They relied on the language of Entry 50 which reads as follows: "taxes on mineral rights subject to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development" and contended that the levy in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy is made under a law made by the Central Legislature on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 304(b) applies.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the Sangunatha Ammal Community and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The respondents took the matter in appeal to the Madras High Court which allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge Nagapattinam. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the succession is "regulated by usage", and (ii) that according to the usage of the deity the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meet of the members Of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [431C] (b) It is not possible to say that there was a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, it is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. [432D E] (c) In the present case there is no warrant for this argument. The phrase "regulated By usage" in section 6 (9) would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present ease is for a fixed period of time and not for life.

The appellant was the village Munsif (Headman). On April 26, 1971 at about 10.00 P.M., he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15) at No. 9. The younger brother of the deceased, Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 p.m. On hearing the shout of his deceased brother crying "younger brother", he ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sitting and fell down on the southern side of a sluice of the north Boothagudi channel, which was shown at No 5 in the place plan (Exhibit P 15). The electric lights were burning in the vicinity He also saw two persons running ahead of accused Karunakaran. He further saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1) and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3) along with Ramasamy (PW 2), chasing them. He ran to their elder brother whom came from behind. The electric light were burning. He also seen the two accused running ahead. He was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. On the prayer of the prosecution, the case against the first two accused without absconding accused was taken up for trial. The two accused were charged under section 120B read with sections 302 and 109 I.P.C. as well as under section 302/34 IPC. The case was referred to the High Court as usual and the accused also preferred appeals against their conviction and sentence. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and accepted the reference in respect of the present accused. His appeal was also dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. It is not possible to adopt that course in this case where the testimony of the sole witness has been rejected with reference to the first accused who was on the same boat with the appellant. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased younger brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that we find that the High court has not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW 4. It failed to notice certain broad facts which should definitely weigh with the Court while appreciating ocular testimony. From the medical evidence it is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness might not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence. But the fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Damodaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical ' evidence. Besides, he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running away after the assault is true, it is difficult to appreciate that he would not mention about this fact in the First Information Report. He admitted in the course of cross examination that the Sub Inspector asked him whether he had any witnesses and that he "did not tell about them due to excitement".

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. Amarchand died on July 7, 1949. Thereafter the partnership was carried on by Mangaldas and Hiralal up to November 30, 1949, and on December 1, 1949 Ramesh son of Amarchand who had by then qualified as a solicitor joined the firm as the third partner. After the death of Amar Chand the arrangement between the various partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of the work done up to the death Of Amarchand the real receipts were to be divided amongst Amarchand, Mangaldas, Hiralal and Ramesh. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. For the five assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 the respondents claimed that they had been assessed to income tax in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives just as the deceased Amarchand would have been had he not died. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34 could validly be served only for the assessment years 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55. On appeal by the respondents the Appellate Tribunal held that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by the heirsand legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under section 24 B(1) of the Income tax Act. On reference the High Court held that apart from section 24E of the Act the amounts were not taxable and that the section had no application to the case. Held, further, that on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the sums which are sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to taxation are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable to be assessed as income (1), 244 Ellis C. Reid vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, , referred to.

Section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 gave power to make rules in respect of certain classes of employment in certain areas. The petitioners who were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad challenged the Act and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. Their case was that Article 16(3) under which the Act, and the Rules purport to be made had been misunderstood as conferring a power to making, a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. For this reason section 3 Of the Act was challenged as ultra rites. Held: (i) The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. The second clause then specifies a prohibition against discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. The intention here is making every office or employment open and available to every citizen, and inter alia to make offices or employment in one part India open to citizens in all other parts of India. (ii) The clause thus enables Parliament to make a law in a special case prescribing any requirement as regards residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment, in the State and to remove ambiguity in language. 120 (iii) There can be no discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. Realising, however that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States might have to he prevented, and a residential qualification may, therefore, have to been prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made. Even so, that clause speaks of residence within tho State. The claim for supremacy of Parliament is misconceived. Par liament in this case as in other matters, is supreme only in so far as the Constitution makes it. Where the Constitution does not concede supremacy, Parliament must act within its appointed functions and not transgress them. What the Constitution says is a matter for,construction of the language of the Constitution which is the proper construction of the two suggested? By the first clause equality of opportunity in employment or appointment to an office is guaranteed. By the second clause there can be any discrimination among others on the basis of residence or its duration rather than its location within the state. (iv) The claim of Mr. Setalvad that Parliament can make a provision regarding residence in any particular part of the State would render the general prohibition lose all its meaning.

The appellant who was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them also for offences tinder sections 467 and 471 of the Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him of all these offences. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals for offences thereunder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; (ii) that in examining the appellant the Sub Inspector did not comply with the requirements of section 342 of the code of Criminal Proce dure; and (iii) that he had an opportunity to get at the articles lost all significance and could possibly have no bearing on the question as to the nature of possession attributable to the appellant. HELD : (i)(a) The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees. It was probably for this reason that the definition clearly lays down that until an article despatched by post is delivered or can be said to be delivered that it will be deemed to be 'in course of trans portation. [416 E F] (b) In a case like the present, what has been established by the prosecution would sustain an inference of secreting. Further, a perusal of section 55 makes it clear that where the entrustment of an article is made an ingredient of an offence, the legislature has used appropriate words to make the matter clear. If, therefore, it was the intention of the Legislature that for an officer of the post office to be punished for secreting, destroying or throwing away a postal Article in the oucrse of transmission by post, entrustment of that article to him was essential it would have used language similar to that used by it in section 55. It seems to us that bearing in mind the fact that an officer has in the course of his duties access to postal articles kept or lying in the post Office, the Legislature has deliberately enlarged the scope of section 52 so as to encompass secretion, destruction etc., of postal article by an officer even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the are riot articles with which he is required or is competent to deal in the way of his duty. [417 F G] (c) The object of the provision is to prevent postal articles 'in the course Of transmission by Post ' from being tampered with, and so the secreting etc., would frustrate or tend to frustrate their delivery to the addressees. Then there can be no doubt that if entrustment were proved and the article entrusted is not found to have been disposed of in the manner permissible under the Act, the offence committed would be not theft but criminal breach of trust.

The appellants filed a complaint before the Nyaya Panchayat, Jokha Khas, District Deoria alleging that he had been abused and be laboured and his property worth Rs. 40/ damaged. On September 10, 1963, Mahabir made an application under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, to transfer the proceedings on the ground that the complainant Yashoda was father of Bunna Prasad, Sarpanch of Nyaya Panchayat Joka Khas. On November 28, 1963 the S.D.M. rejected this application and on December 13, 1963 a notice was issued to the five members of the Panchayat to assemble on December 25, 1963 and hear the case. On December 20, 1963 Mahabir moved an application before the Magistrate alleging that "writ petition has been admitted and a stay order has been issued. But despite his informing the Panchayat Adalat of that, I am not getting any hearing there, and when an application is made there, it was not entertained". The appellant, who was sleeping in his cattle shed in village Bhadurpur Ghar, with a sword at about mid night on the night between June 14 15, 1960. Sheo Sahai died of the injuries received by him. The prosecution case was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and asked him to go to the Police Station, Ekdil, nine miles away and lodged a report. He delivered the sword which had been found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood. The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of investigation was sent up for trial, The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge believed Ujagar Singh and acted on the extra judicial confession made by the appellant to him. Both the Courts below concurrently found that the evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive, to his extrajudicial confession to one Ujagar Singh when he was having a bath in the Canal at that hour of the night cannot be said to be improbable. The High Court also did not rely on this extra judicial confessional confession. It relied on certain statements made by him in his report dictated at the Police station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant 's conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed. The murder was committed in the month of June.

For the purpose of holding election to the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the month of December, 1978 under the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation Act, 1956 (No. 23 of 1956) (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act '), the Collector published the preliminary electoral roll on September 30, 1978 and notified that the poll if necessary would take place on December 31, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on December 28, 1978 requesting the court to make an order quashing the electoral roll and the calendar of events issued for the purpose. The learned Single Judge before whom the case came up for orders directed the issue of notice of the petition and the stay application to the respondents and issued an interim order directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the Rules pending disposal of the writ petition. On December 31. 1978, the poll was held and 44 persons were declared elected. Their names were, however, not published under rule 46 of Rules in view of the interim order made by the Court. Thereafter the successful candidates were also impleaded as respondents and the petition was amended by inclusion of an additional prayer that the declaration of results of all the 43 successful candidates should be quashed. After the respondents filed their counter affidavits, the petition being heard and it was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High court on January 20, 1979.

The respondent company filed a complaint against the appellant company and its directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section. Admittedly no general body meeting had been held and, therefore, the balance sheets and profit & loss account had not been laid before a general body Meeting nor could it be so laid. The Full Bench speaking through Jaganmohan Reddy, C.J., as his brother then was, held that if no balance sheet is laid before the general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balancesheet and profit account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the principle accepted by this Court in The State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors. ; , and that a company or its directors in a prosecution under section 32 and section 133 of the Companies Act could not in defence to such prosecution rely upon their own failure to call the general Body meeting as a defence to the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) On principle and authority it should be held that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134. They might have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 but not under section134. [416E F] (2) Section 134 lays down that after balance sheet & profit and losses account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, have been laid, before the company at the general meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to do so is made punishable under section 135(4). The difference in language is very clear and pointed. The responsibility of sending three copies of the balance Sheet and profit or loss account or income and the expenditure account as the ease may be arises only after they have been placed before the Company at the meeting. Without so laying copies could not be sent to the Registrar and even if they are sent it would not be a compliance with the provisions Of section 134.[416G H] (3)(a) In construing a penal provision it is not permissible to give an extended meaning to the plain words of the section on the ground that a principle recognised in respect of certain other provisions is inconsistent with the principle as embodied a certain other sections which are differently worded. [419A B] (b) The court there observed that this is not a case where an accused person relies on his default and pleads his innocence. What he says is, I may have committed an offence but the offence that I have committed is not the one with which I am charged. On the facts proved by the prosecution an offence is not disclosed under section 26(4), but it appears to us that there is a very clear distinction between sections 32 and 133 on the one hand and section 134 on the other. Section 32 relates to the preparation of a list of members of the Company and of persons who have ceased to be members as well as a summary, and also provides that it shall be completed within 21 days after the day of the first or only ordinary general meeting in the year. It further provides that the company shall forthwith file with the Reserve Bank a copy of the list and summary, any default hi complying with this requirement is made penal by the Act. [414C D] (4) The liability to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meetings.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal by a notification dated 26th January 1950 in exercise of the powers conferred by section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special Judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 (1), under which it was sent to that court for trial, was unconventional and void under article 13(2)as it denied to the respondent the equal protection of laws enjoined by article 14. The High Court quashed the conviction but directed the trial of the respondent and other accused persons according to law. Hence the appeal. Held: (i) The classification implied in this part of the sub section has no reference to, and is not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but is concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of cases". (ii) The object by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences or the cases, for, in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis tinguish one offence or one class of offences from another offence, or class of cases, speedier trial is desirable in the disposal of all offences or classes of offences. (iii) The State can, under section 269(1), do away with trial by jury but that does not mean that judges are to deter mine what is for the good of the people and substitute their individual and personal opinions for that of the Government of the day, or that they may usurp the functions of the legislature.

The Central Health Service was formed more than two decades ago and was intended to replace the Indian Medical Service, but the recruitment rules were not framed till the year 1963. The service was constituted for providing doctors for manning the medical, public health and medical research and teaching posts in the Central Government hospitals, dispensaries scientific research institutions and institutions of higher education. The members of this Service are also meant to man posts in Union Territories and the various autonomous bodies. In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution, the President on May 1, 1963 made the Central Health Services (Amendment) Rules, 1966 which came into force 18 May 5, 1963. R.3 provided for the constitution of the Central health Service. Under r. 4(2), the controlling authority had the power to interchange any post included in the junior scale with any post including in the senior scale without altering the authorized strength in each category. R8 provided for 50% of the vacancies in Category 'B ' of the supertime scale were to be filled by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the post in the Senior Scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that scale and 20% of vacancies thereof were to he filled by direct recruitment in the manner specified in the Second Schedule. By a notification dated January 1, 1965, the initial appointments were notified. The essential pre condition for the inclusion of a post in a Central Health service was that a medical qualification recognised under the Indian medical Council should be prescribed for it. By the Central Heath Service (Amendment), Rules 1966, the Central Medical Health Service ( Amendment) Rules 1966 was reorganized with effect from September 9, 1966 and the concept of General Duty officers and Specialist Grade Officers was introduced for the first time. R .8(2A) and paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second schedule provided that every vacancy in the Specialists ' Grade shall be filled up by promotion from amongst persons holding the posts of Associate Professor or Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality in a medical college/teaching institution after the requisite post graduate qualification is absolutely essential. The appellant was not only holding the Post of Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital but was also actively associated with teaching the under graduate and post graduate students as an Associate Professor of Radiology (ex officio) in the Maulana Azad Medical College. On August 19/20, 1968, the Principal, Maulana Gandhi Medical College addressed a letter to the appellant conveying that the Vice Chancellor of the Delhi University in exercise of his emergency powers had granted him recognition as an Assistant Professor of radiotherapy for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students for the D.M.R.T. and M.B.S. courses of studies. The Ministry of Health by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the Secretary (Medical), Delhi Administration that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist, in the Medical College, and that consequent upon the appointment of the appellant in Category `C ' of tho Central Health Serv ice, the Administration had no objection to designating him as Associate Professor. The Government of India, Ministry of Finance by its order dated January 17, 1976 informed the Delhi Administration, that it would not be possible to relieving the appellant from his duties and place his service on deputation alongwith a lien in his post, as Radiology in Maulana Ali Medical College with effect From October 9, 1964, the appellant was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview on August 7, 1972 for the post of Professor of Pathotherapy but since the post was falling vacant in 1973, he did not appear for the interview. The government of India Ministry of health and Family Planning Department by its Letter dated February 3, 1974 intimated the Delhi Adminis tration that it had no objections to designing him as a Associate Professor and no financial implications were involved.

An industrial dispute between the workmen and the management of Orient Paper Mills Ltd. (the Company) was referred by the State Government under section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication by the Tribunal enumerating 30 different items of dispute. The Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items. The special leave in this Court was sought and granted in respect of two matters covering some of these items. On behalf of the workmen it was urged that (1) there should be greater emphasis on the region part of the industry cum region principle, though it would be the duty of the industrial court to see that for purposes of comparison such other industries in the region are taken into account as are nearly similar to the concern before it; and (2) even in adopting the latter course, the Tribunal committed an error inasmuch as, in making the calculation, the tribunal only tried to neutralise about 36 per cent of the cost of living. HELD : (1)(a) There is no justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which is the average minimum wage payable by those industries (1 ) [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 673, followed. (b) The Tribunal committed any error in arriving at this decision and, consequently, the total minimum wage fixed by it must also be deemed to have the same break up. As a result, it would have to be held that the total wage packet which a workman should be entitled to receive was fixed by the tribunal at Rs. 95. From the facts noted in the Award or appearing on the record, it appears that production bonus, in addition to the minimum wage, is payable in the case of Aluminium Company, Hirakud; but there does not appear to be any production bonus payable in this three Collieries, in the Steel Plant and in the Cement Factory. In the majority of the industries which are being compared with the Company in the Region, consequently the minimum wages prevailing in these concerns were (1)[1963] Suppl. 2 S. C. R. 673 and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed, as that year was still running when the award was given by the Tribu nal on the 11th January, 1964. Further, there is no extra amount received as production bonus. It is only in those cases that the bonus is worked out on the basis of the total basic wage, because it cannot be assumed that their wage is a consolidated wage consisting of the two elements of basic wage and dearness allowance.

Section 25(4) of the Income tax Act, 1922, provides that where any business, profession or vocation on which tax was at any time charged under the provisions of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, is discontinued, then unless there has been a succession by virtue of which the provisions Of sub section (4) have been rendered applicable no tax shall be payable in respect of the income, profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of such discontinuance. Section 25(3) provides that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1918. The appellant claimed relief under section 25(1) contending that it had transferred its business to a limited company with effect either from November 13, 1947 or February 13, 1948, by an instrument executed on February 7, 1948. The claim was rejected by the Income Tax Officer and by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also by the Incometax Appellate Tribunal on appeal to this Court. HELD: (i) Under section 25 (4), a mere change in the constitution of the partnership does not count and sections 25(2) and 26 (2) do not apply at the same time, because the intention is obviously to keep them separate and when sub section 4 was added, sub section 3 was amended by the addition of the words "unless there has already been a devolution by virtue Of which the provi sions of sub section 2 have been made applicable. The business which had been subjected to tax in 1939 had been discontinued in October/November 1937 or on May 30, 1939 and it was not in existence in 1948 so as to permit a succession to it taking place under the instrument of February 7. [108 E F] (ii) Under sub section(4), the business could be said to have ceased. The income tax Act does not in terms of joint family business but in terms Of business in a business sense, and it is the business which was taxed under the Act of 1918 which must cease to exist before the benefit of section 25 can be obtained. It is possible that the decision might be justified on the ground that the benefit was being claimed by one of the members of the erstwhile family and not by the whole family, though I express no opinion upon it, but even so that would be a case of succession rather than of discontinuance. The Madras case cannot, however, be made applicable to the present facts because, as pointed out already by me, there was no cessation of business in so far as the original business of piece goods, yarn and banking was concerned.

The plaintiff 's suit based as it was on the provisions of section 6, is essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary property. Two things become necessary to determine for the purpose of giving relief to the plaintiff. One, her share in her husband 's share and two, their husband ' own share in it. The proviso to section 6 comes into play and the normal rule is excluded. Khandappa 's interest in the Mitakshara coparcenary property would devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with the provisions Of the Act. But, since the widow and daughter are amongst the female relatives specified in class I of the Schedule to the Act and Khandappa died leaving behind a widow and daughters, the proviso to s.6 comes into operation and the ordinary rule is exclusion of other heirs. Testamentary successive is out of question as the deceased had not made a testamentary disposition though under the explanation to section 30 of the Act, the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary Property is capable of being disposed of by a will or other testamentary disposition. There is thus no dispute that the normal Rule provided for by section 6 does not apply, that the proviso is attracted and that the decision of the appeal must turn on the meaning to be given to Explanation 1 of section6. The interpretation of Explanation I thereto will further the legislative intent in regard to the enlargement of the share of female heirs, qualitatively and quantitatively. The Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 conferred heirship rights on the son 's daughter, daughter 's sister and sister in all areas where the Mitakshara law prevailed. Section 3 of the Hindu Women 's Rights to Property Act, 1937, provides that any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of the 1956 Act, shall be held by her as a full owner thereof and not as a limited owner. By restricting the operation of the fiction created by Explanation I in the manner suggested by the appellant, it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain the share, of the deceased in the coparcener property, one cannot go back on that assumption and ascertain the shares of the heirs without reference to it. [764 H; 765 A B] (2) The assumption which the statute requires to be made that a partition had in fact taken place must permeate the entire process of ascertainment of the ultimate share of the heir, through all its stages. To make the assumption at the initial stage for the limited purpose of ascertaining the share Of the deceased and then to ignore it for calculating the quantum of the shares is truly to permit one 's imagination to boggle. All the consequences which flow from a real partition have to be logically worked out, which means that the share must be ascertained on the basis that they bad separated from one another and had received a share In the instant case, by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Indian Succession Act, it was not necessary for the purposes of working out the fiction, to assume and supply a missing link which is really what was meant by Lord Asquith in his famous passage in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. vs Finsbury Borough Council ([1959] Stipp. 1 S.C.R.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial interest of a Judge. The letter also concluded by saying that the Honble Judge during his entire stay in his tour deliberately showed the bent of his mind towards commu nism while exchanging view on various matters. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of the Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri. Each of the appellants affirmed an affidavit in this pattern. It is an article of faith with the deponent that dignity and respect of all Courts and of all Judges and particularly of the High Court must be maintained for, amongst other reasons, on that depends the orderly function ing of the society as also prestige of the profession to which the deponent has the honour to belong. The deponent has been taught to believe that a Judge ought always to steer clear of all avoidable controversial matters. In order to prevent unwanted disclosure of its contents, the communica tion in question was brought personally by two members of Bar Association Bhiwani to Chandigarh in a closed cover addressed to the Chief Justice for being handed over to him for his personal attention. The respondent submitted that the contents of the letter did not bear out any foundation for an action for criminal contempt. In any case, if in view of this Hon ' Court, the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. Therefore, the deponent tenders his apology to this Honble Court, for the same and prayed for its acceptance. The Full Bench of the Punjab High Court consisting of Justice Surjit Singh Sandhawalia, Justice Prem Chand Jain and Jus tice Bhupinder Singh Dhillon extracted portions from the affidavit of the appel lant to which references have been made.

Section 5(1) of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, provides that no person shall be entitled to inspect, call for or obtain copies of any documents, statement or papers or materials furnished to, obtained by or produced before the Commission or any authorised official in any proceedings under this Act. The Central Government referred these cases to the Investigation Commission appointed under the provisions of section 5(4) of that Act and these were numbered 831/64 69 on the records of the Commission and during the investigation of some other cases similarly referred to the Commission, it was said to have been discovered that the petitioner company had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thus evaded taxa tion. On the 28th August, 1953, a report to this effect was made by the Commission to the Central Government under section 5 (4) requesting that the case of the petitioner along with the cases of Suraj Mall Mohta and other members of his family may be referred to a Commission for investigation. The Commission notified the petitioners that their cases had been referred for investigation and they were called upon to furnish certain material, as detailed in Annexure "B" of the petition, to the commission. On September 12, 1953 the Commission notified them that their case had been forwarded for investigation under section 6(4). On the 15th of September, 1953 a report was made to this Court by the Central Govern ment under section 7(3) requesting the Commission for the withdrawal of any case or points in a case which the Central Govt. had prima facie reasons for believing that a person has evaded payment of taxation on income, together with such material as may be available in support of such belief and may at any time before the 1st day of September 1948, apply to the Commis sioner for withdrawal of the case or point in a Case thus referred. The petitioners contended (i) that sections 5(3), 6, 7 and 8 of the Act were void as being discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the Constitution of India by reason of article 14 of the Constitu tion; (ii) that there was no substantial difference in procedure prescribed under section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act and the impugned Act and that in any case the procedure prescribed by the Act was a good substitute for that prescribed by it the Indian income tax Act. Held, that both sections 34 of Indian Income Tax Act and sub section (4)(a) of section 6 of the impugned act deal with all persons who have similar characteristics and similar properties, the common characteristics being that they are persons who had not truly disclosed their income and have evaded payment Of taxation on Income. It was not possible to hold that all such persons who evade payment of income tax and do not truly disclose all particulars or material facts necessary for their assessment and against whom a report is made under sub section(4)(b) of s 5 of the said Act by themselves form a class distinct from those who evaded payment, of income Tax and come within the ambit of section 34 Of the Indian Incometax Act.

They read " Commercial Establishment" means any premises wherein any trade, business or profession or any work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary thereto is carried on but does not include a shop or a factory registered under the , or theaters, cinemas, restaurants eating houses, residential hotels, clubs or other places of public amusement or entertainment to which this Act applies and includes such other establishment as Government may from time to time be fixed by the Federation in addition to the admission fee of Rs. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The activity of the Association is one of general utility; the only source of its income is from subscriptions.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. By a Treaty between the East India Company Nawab Asfuddaula in or about the year 1775, the province of Benares was ceded to British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhittery in perpetuity to Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the Jagir and became entitled to merely a pension. The letter by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8 is dated July 7, 1837 and was from H. Elliot Esqr., the Secretary Sadar Board of Revenue N.W.P. Allahabad, to J. Thompson Esqrs., Offg. Secretary to Lt. Government, N. W.P., Allahabad, who held that the amount which had been received by the successors of Babu Harnarain Singh varied from year to year and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. It relied on the fact that the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, but the immediate and effective source is rent, which has suffered the accident of nonpayment. The allowance was in a sense related to the land revenue assessed on the land i.e., it was fixed as a percentage of the land Revenue; but the percentage was merely a measure, and indicated the source of this right in lieu of which the allowance was given. It was contended that if the assessee 's predecessor had received compensation for relinquishing his title to the lands in dispute, that would have been a capital receipt and not taxable. Held, further, that the allowance is revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income.

In exercise of its powers under section 63(7) of the , the Central Government specified 50 as the number of 'All India Tourist Vehicle Permits ' which may be granted by the Karnataka State Transport Authority. By section 24 of Amending Act 47 of 1978, a proviso to section 63 (7) was introduced whereby permits had been granted by Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and 14 remained to be granted. There were as many as 496 applications for the grant of these 14 permits. By an order dated February 1, 1984, the Supreme Court directed the Karnataka state Transport Authority to dispose of these applications. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal set aside the grant in favour of the Karnataka Tourism Development Corporation and instead granted three permits to private operators and increased the number and of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tion from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to Section 63( 7), the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the numbers of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number Of permits to be issued. It was on that ground that the grant had been set aside, though the Appellate Tribunal had no doubt regarding the resources and ability of that Corporation to operate the tourist services. The High Court also took the same view in Sher Singh 's case and that the fourth sub clause of the proviso offended article 14 and had to he struck down. Allowing the appeals by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tho State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. Except in the cases of a specified notified route, the application of no applicant may be altogether excluded from consideration on the sole ground that another applicant is entitled to preference under one or the other provisions of the statute. The proviso to sec. 63(1), for example, provides that other conditions being equal, an application for stage carriage permit from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall as far as may be, be given priority over applications from individual owners. There is no question of eliminating private operators merely because the Undertaking applies for a stage carriage permits under Chapter IV. In an application under chapter IV, Corporation has to enter into the arena like any other applicant, face the competition and come up to the level of other private operators intending to obtain stage carriage Permit and then in respect of the route in question claim preference.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50 The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 6 63 denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the Madras High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ in the nature of certiorari to quash the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under sections 19(1) and (2) of the Madras General Sales tax Act, 1939. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that upon a true construction of the registered instrument the respondent undertook to pay not only Sch. I liabilities but also other liabilities like sales tax imposed in regard to the business; and (ii) that there was no contractual obligation between the transferor and the transferee and the State Govern ment who is not a party to the instrument. HELD: (1) The word 'assessment ' used in section 19(2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule21 A is beyond the rulemaking power of State Government either under section 19 or section 19 (2)(C) of tho Act. [665 C] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; and Chatturam vs C I.T. Bihar, , relied on. (2). The word "assessment" in the scheme of sales Tax and income tax legislation is a term of varying import. The word is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. As the Judicial Committee, however, said in Badridassas Daga 's case it did not follow 7 that there is a liability created inter se between the State Govt. on the one hand and the transferor on the other hand. [66 B C] (3) In the present case the registered document by which the business was transferred to the respondent was dated October May 5, 1955 and the amending Act had therefore no application. [664 G] Baddridas Chettiar Daga vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, ; , referred to.

The plaintiff entered service in the Gondal State in 1927 as a jailor. He was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant at Rajkot Central Prison. On March 7, 1954, he was served with a charge sheet. In substance the charges were that while he was serving at Surendranagar he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The plaintiff filed a written statement on September 4, 1954 and an enquiry was held by Mr. Gangopadhyay. The Enquiry Officer made a report and on or about January 7, 1955, the following notice was issued to him calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service "To Shri Bhaishanker A. Joshi, Accountant, Rajkot Central Jail (Under suspension) Charges framed against you under this office No. C/ 14 dated 27 3 54 and in particular the charges of having accepted illegal gratificationfrom prisoner Ratilal Jivan have been established to the satisfaction of Government. You are hereby asked to showcause why the punishment of dismissal from service should not he inflicted upon you. He should submit his reply to this office, through the Superintendent, Rajkot, Central Prison within a week from the date of receipt of this letter without fail. Sd/ M J. BHATT Inspector General of Prisons, Government of Saurashtra. " The plaintiff appeared before the Enquiry Officer and cross examined witnesses. He also examined himself and some witnesses. The enquiry officer made a further report and held that the plaintiff was dismissed from serv ice on account of charge of accepting illegal gratification by prisoner Rati Lal Jivan having been conclusively proved against him in the departmental inquiries conducted against him by the Government. On appeal, the District Judge, Central Saurashtra held that there had been a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against him and consequently he had not been given reasonable opportunity within the meaning of Article 311 (2). The plaintiff appealed to the High Court claiming arrears of salary and the State of Bombay filed cross objections praying that the suit be dismissed. The second appeal was heard by the High court who directed that the decree passed by the lower appellate court "be varied so as to show that the appellant continued to be in Government service till the date when the suit only and there will be a decree for Rs. 2,690 919 being arrears of pay due to the plaintiff upto the date on which the suit was filed. The High Court held that (1) the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy Of the report by the Enquiry officer amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311 (3); and (2) there had thus been a violation of article 14 of the constitution. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the liability to pay arrears of wages was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract. HELD : The High court came to a correct conclu sion and held against the State Government. [921 C] (1)(a) It is true that the question whether reasonable opportunity has or has not been afforded to the Government servant must depend on the facts of each case, but it would be in very rare cases indeed in which it could be said that the Government Servant was not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of report of Enquiry Officer.
