The appellant granted a lease of the coal and coal mining rights in respect of 400 bighas out of 592 bighas to one Jugal Kishore Lal. Samanta bad surrendered his rights under the previous lease in favour of the Raja and taken a fresh lease of it on a reduced rent. On June 10, 1901, Jugal Kishore Lai gave a fresh grant of the same holding to Samanta and incorporated a map in that lease, i.e., exhibit 3(b). There, the northern boundary of the appellant 's leasehold land was shown as the northern boundaries of the leasehold land of Samanta. The plan, exhibit 3 (b), annexed to this lease deed showed the boundary line between the two leaseholds. The said map was drawn to scale and incorporated in the lease deed, it is clear from the plan that the southern boundary of this plot is conterminous with the northern demarcation of the respondents ' leasehold land in favour Of Samanta, and it appears that Samanta purchased the interest of Banerji in the leasehold of 1894 and thereafter at the request of Samanda, on November 23, 1900, the appellant made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. On those allegations, they asked for the following reliefs: (a) That the intermediate boundary line from the appellants ' coal land be ascertained and fixed; (b)That a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the plaintiffs ' coal lands and cutting and removing coal therefrom. (c) That an enquiry be made and the quantity of coal cut and removed by the defendants be ascertained, and a decree for the value thereof by way of damages be granted to the plaintiffs against the defendant. The respondents denied that they had encroached on any portion of their coal Mines. The trial court held that article 48 of the Limitation Act applied to the suit and that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of it since 1932 when there was a survey by the Department of Mines. On appeal, the High Court accepted all the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The finding of the courts below is vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. It is well settled that a map referred to in a lease should be treated as incorporated in it and as forming part of the said document. In this case, the maps accepted by the High court are drawn to scales and the boundary is clearly demarcated. The question really is one of fact and we accept the finding. The encroachment by the appellant on the respondents colliery and the removal of coal therefrom are alleged to have taken place in or about the year 1932. (ii) It is not permissible for a Court to reconstruct the plan with reference to revenue records when the plan is self contained and drawn to Scale.

The appellant, a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It is said that he came again a short time later at 4 30 p.m. and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. Sankaran gave an explanation the same day denying the allegations of fact made against him though he admitted that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. On June 25, 1958 Sankaran was informed by Sankaran that in view of his denial a departmental inquiry would be held and he was also placed under suspension pending enquiry. The same day Sankaran protested against his suspension and requested that in any case the departmental inquiry should be expedited. As no inquiry was held till July 2, 1958, Sankaran again wrote to the appellant to hold the inquiry as early as possible. On July 8, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental enquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran the same date. In that order the appellant informed Sankaran that the proposed inquiry, if conducted, would lead to further friction and deterioration in the rank and file of the employees in general and also that maintenance of discipline in the undertaking would be prejudiced if he was retained in the service of the appel lant, and therefore it considered that no enquiry should be held. A dispute was then raised by the union which was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication by the Government of Kerala in October 1958. The tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21, 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r . 18(b) of Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the tribunal in connection with the alleged offence, but the tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer of the Secretary, and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The Industrial Tribunal therefore held that on the facts it could not come to its conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the Mill and abused or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or the other officers. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Where the termination of service is capricious, arbitrary or unnecessarily harsh on the part of the employer judged by normal standards of a reasonable man that may be cogent evidence of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. (ii) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of services even under a rule like 18(A) and if it is satisfied that the action was bona fide and was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation, or unfair Labour practice, it would have jurisdiction to interfere. (iii) Where an employer wanted to take action for misconduct and then suddenly dropped the departmental proceedings which were intended to be held, and decided to discharge the employee under r, 18(c).

By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Faraqui on the one hand and Messrs. Filmistan Distributors (India) Private Ltd., hereinafter called "Filmistan" instituted a suit in the Court of Small Causes at Ahmedabad against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated October 27,1954, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By an order dated December 1, 1960, the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and Eraqui were bound and liable to allow Filmisten to exercise its "exhibition rights" in the cinema theatre; that Raval, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibit any picture in contravention of the terms and conditions of the agreement. On September 1, 1963, Filmistansan filed a suit No. 1465 of 1963 in the court of Small Cause at Ahmedabad inter alia for declaration that as sub lessee or as lessee under law it was enti tled to obtain and remain in possession of the theatre and to exhibit cinematograph films and to hold "entertainment performances" etc., in the Theatre, and that one Shabeer Hussain Khan Tejabwala had no right, title or interest in the Cinema theatre, that the defendants in the suit be ordered to hand over vacant and peaceful possession of it and the defendants, their agents and servants be restrained by an injunction from interfering directly or indirectly with its rights to obtain or remain in posses sion of the Theatre or any part thereof and to exercise their right of exhibiting "motion pictures" and entertainment etc. The suit was based on the claim made by Filmiston as lessees or sub lessees of the cinema, against Raval & Faraqqui and two others claiming a declara tion that it had been entitled pursuant thereto to the agreements dated November 26, 1954 to exhibit Motion pictures in their theatre. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the revision petition holding that the question asked in cross examination of the witnesses for Filmisthan intended to secure disclosure of the surrounding circumstances and conduct of the parties in order to show in what manner the language of the document was related to the existing facts, could not be excluded. The High Court also rejected the contention that there was any bar of estoppel, and held that evidence as to the true nature of the transaction was not inadmissible by virtue of section 92 of the Evidence Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of Filmistnecan that an enquiry into the nature of legal relationship arising out of the said agreement could be permitted to 'be put to a witness who was being examined, no case was decided by the trial court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant; that in any event the case or any portion thereof was not likely to be disposed of on these issues and that ordinarily in "appealable cases" the Court should, as far as possible decide all the issues together and that piecemeal trial might result in protracting the litigation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. 442 This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, ; that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import; it includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Code to the extent to which the court, viz., the trial Court in the instant case, proposed to go into that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1. 1960, to be reopened, it is proposing to exercise the jurisdiction which is not vested in it by law. It is not open to any court of law to try an issue over again or reopen the same if an earlier decision operates as res judicata.

The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Chittoor of an offence under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. An order of acquittal can be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial", and compelling reason". However, such expressions have been used more as flourishes of language, to emphasise the reluctance of the Appellate Court to interfere with an order of conviction than to curtail the power of the appellate court to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion. [368C E] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of U.P., A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460, approved. Sanwat singh & Ors vs State Of Rajasthan, A.l. R. 1971 SC 460, referred to. In the instant case, the High Court was right in holding that the medical evidence supported the prosecution version and not the defence version. Merely because the Medical Officer stated that the victim could have received the injury if she was standing, it did not follow that the injury could have been received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused. The injury was inflicted with great force and its direction was upward. The location of the injury was 6 cms below the arm pit on the left side. According to the accused, the deceased received the injuries when she placed herself between P. W. 1 and himself. Therefore, it could not be said that an injury of the nature received by the deceased could have caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [369E F] Sanchal Singh & Anr.

Section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 provides that a public servant denotes a person falling under any of the descrip tion mentioned therein: "Third Every Judge including any person empowered by law to discharge, whether by himself or as a member of any body of persons any adjudicarory functions. " The definition of a public Servant is very wide enough to include Judges of the Supreme Court as well as judges of the High Court. Section 77 of the Indian Penal Code provides immunity to the Judges in respect of any act done by a Judge when acting judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law. The President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of the 'High Court from his office except with the previous sanction under clause (c) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his Office. The power to punish a High Court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of the Constitu tion, under which a Judge of the high Court can be removed from his offices by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The third most important question which falls for decision in this case is whether a Judge will be liable for committing criminal misconduct within the meaning of clause (e) of sub section (1) of Section 5 of the Act if he has in his possession pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income for which the public servant cannot satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources and property disproportionate lo his known source of income. ^ HELD: 1. The Constitution while providing that their position would be akin to that of a Judge who may be a public servants according to the wide definition of the expression in the Act but whose category for the grant of sanction for prosecution is not envisaged by Section 6, it is not intended to be covered by the Act. It is for this reason that the learned Solicitor General did not place reliance on clauses (a) and(b) of Sub section (I) of Sec tion 6 in the present case but relied on clause (C) thereof, to contend that sanction thereunder can be obtained for the prosecution of a judge or Chief Justice of a High ' Court since the holder of such an office can be removal from his post by the President. The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were the members of a scheduled caste. An election to a seat in the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidabad constitutency reserved for members of the Scheduled Castes. The contestants at this election were Abhiman Pada, a member belonging to the Sunri caste which was a Scheduled caste. Sudhir objected to this nomination contending that Abhonoy Paada did not belong to any Scheduled Caste and that it was, therefore, not c open to him at the trial to contend, as he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition on the ground that he did not belongs to a Scheduled Castes specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the word "excluding" denoted that the Sahas contemplated would, but for this word have come within the Suniti caste, no question of Sahas being a distinct class independent of Sunriscould arise; and (ii) that in view of the fact that the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 was promulgated to indicate those castes who were to be considered as Scheduled Castes for the purpose of the Constitution. HELD: (1) The Tribunal came to its conclusion that it had not been prov ed in this case that the appellant belonged to any separate Saha caste or to any Saha Sunri sub caste of the Sunras caste. [390 C] (2) It was open to the respondent to show that the expression "excluding Sahas" meant excluding a smaller Caste group called Sahas, and it would have read "Sunri excluding those who bore the surname Saha. In the absence of such words "Saha ' must, in the context, be understood as referring to a larger caste group within the bigger caste group Of Sunris. [391 E F] (3) It is natural to think that when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste, the other must be a caste. It follows that when the item excluded Sahas from Sunris, since Sunri is a Caste group, Saha must equally be another caste group. [392 G] (4) The appellant was not a Sunri by caste and has not been proved to belong to the Scheduled Caste specified in Item 40 for greater safety o prevent them from claiming to be Sunris by reason of their origin.

The complainant actually paid the accused two sums of money on 7th November 1948 and 17th November, 1948. He, however, got into contact with the police on 1 12 1948 and in conjunction with the latter a trap was laid for the appellant. It was arranged that the complaint should bring with him Rs. 1,000 being the balance due in respect of the furniture and that he agreed to give him Rs 29, 500 to be paid back on the appellant 's return to India. The police party who were down below ready for the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of RS. 30500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement was tween the complainant and the appel lant and an application form for permission to occupy the building as caretaker. From the complainant were recovered the bunch of keys and the documents that were handed over to him by the appellant, namely, the letter handing vacant possession (Exhibit D). The receipt for Rs. 2,500 for the articles of furniture (Exhibit E), a letter to the Bombay Gas Company for transfer of the gas connection to the name of the complainant (Exhib it F) and the letter to Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Committee for transfer Of the telephone connec tions and the deposit of Rs 27 (Exhibit G). The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, LVII of 1947 for receiving a pugree of Rs 29500 and he was further charged under s.19(2) of that Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appe lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caRetaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. The sum of money was not pugna ble but represented capital for 0 12 0 share in the business and as the complainant 's brother, threw off his disguise and disclosed his identity. The Presidency Magistrate who tried the case dis missed the defence on the ground that what was received by the accused was by way of pugriree. As section 18 (1) was not applicable he convicted him under section 19(2). He preferred an appeal to the High Court but it was summarily dismissed on 20 2 1950. The appellant asked for a certificate under article 134(1)(c) of tile Constitution but this was rejected on 10 4 1950. Thereaf ter he applied for special leave to appeal to this Court and it was granted on 3 10 1950. On 10 1950, the question whether the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or any consideration as a condi tion of the relat quishment by a tenant of his tenant and that in the present case there was no such relinquishment.

The appellant, Tata Consulting Engineers, served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. 170 The Union filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. It was urged that having regard to the financial capacity of the appellant, the Tribunal erred in making the wage scale retrospective and, in any event, in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January, 1976. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the Union for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system, because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the Appellant 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. The Industrial Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appel lant and decided to modify the existing structure of scales with flat increases in each category. But it rejected the claim of the union for dearness allowances on the ground that there would have been a consequent increase in the dearness allowance, and house rent allowance. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the workmen that having due regard to their financial capacity, the Industrial Tribunal erred In making the award dated December 20, 1978, the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs. 150/ to each workman in the case of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in the category of Draftsmen and of Rs., 100/ and Rs, 100/ respectively in the cases of other categories, a result wholly unwarranted, it is said, by the intent of the original award and, therefore, falling beyond the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The terms of reference in the State Govern ment 's order required the Tribunal to revise the scales of pay and dearness allowances, and there were no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in their basic pay of individual workman. The sufficiency of the existing pay scales was considered in detail, and regard was had to their original structure and the accretions made subsequently by way of dearness allowances and house rents allowance. The financial capacity as the Tribunal observed, constituted one of "the principles which are required to be followed in the fixation of the wages structure". A clear statement of its intention is found in paragraph 22 of the award where the Tribunal stated: "I only propose to modify, the existing structures of the scales with flats increase in each categories." The fitment has also to be done only after the flat increase is added to the present basic salary of each employee. One is the retrospectivity attached to the revised wage scale pertaining to different categories. That the increase was the one incorporated in the revised pay scales pertaining to various categories. The amendment made by the Tribunal has the effect of providing a second increase, this time to each individual workmen. If, as the Industrial Tribu nal has stated in the amendment order, the increase in paragraph 23 was intended to apply to each particular individual workman, there is nothing in the body of the Award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales can be made to rest.

Section 2(vi) of the , as it stood at the relevant time, provided that wages means all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money which would, if the terms of the contract of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded did amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant 's to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the res pondents ' claim, which was rejected by the authority holding that section 15 of the Act was applicable to the case because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vii) and it also argued that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The High Court affirmed the finding of the authority and held that the applications made by the respond ent were competent under section 15 Of the Act before the Patna High Court by filing a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section 2 (vi) cannot take in the wages prescribed under the award is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structure prescribed by the Award. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the Award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) Of the , before it was amended. The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection, we may incidentally refer to the decision of this Court in South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1951 Cal. 29 and V. B Godse, Manager, Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act (3), the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudica tion.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co., which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The first respondent claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. This dispute was ultimately referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra. Before the Tribunal the Company resisted the workmen 's claim but submitted that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had already been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age 55 subject to their employee passing a Medical Examination on reaching that age. The Tribunal directed that the age should be 58 but the company may in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was also found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years, and on a closer examination it was clear that this document was of little assistance for finding out the recent trend.

The Company Law Board issued an order on behalf of the company Law Board under section 237(b) of the appointing 4 persons as Inspectors for investigating the affairs of the Barium Chemicals Ltd., appellant No. 1 before us, since its incorporation in the year 1961 and to report to the company law Board inter alia "all the irregularities and contravention in respect of the provisions of or of any other law for the time being in force and the person or persons responsible for such irregularities and breach". The order was made by the Chairman on behalf Of the Board by virtue of the powers conferred on him by certain rules to which we shall refer later. On June 4, 1965, the company preferred a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the Punjab High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus or other appropriate writ, direction or order quashing the order of the Board dated May 19, 1965 and also sought some other incidental reliefs. The writ petition was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that it was made mala fide because no honest opinion was formed on the matters which under the section give rise to the power but on irrelevant and extraneous material, and further because the order was passed under the influence and malice of a Minister of Cabinet who was interested in another Company belonging to his sons and sought this means to oust a rival. Held: (i) The powers are exercised for ascertaining facts and, therefore before they are finally known, all that is necessary for the exercise of the power is the opinion of the board that there are circumstances which suggest to it that fraud and other kinds of mismanagement mentioned in sub cls. T. T., (ii) that persons concerned in the formation of the Company or the management of its affairs have in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company and its members; or (iii) that they have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect including including information relating to the calculation of the commission payable to a managing or other director, the managing agent, the secretaries and treasurers, or the manager of the said Company. By section 237 (b) the power was conferred on the Central Government but under the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1963 a Board of Company Law Administration consisting of a Chairman and a member has been set up. The new sub section involves a delegation of the Powers of the Central Govern ment to a member of the Boards which the Act previously allowed to be made to the Board only. The second is what are the powers of the directors in this behalf and whether they have been exercised contrary to the requirements of the Act. It may be mentioned that in paragraph 16 of the affidavit the Chairman also stated: "With reference to para 21 of the petition, I have already stated above that there was ample material before the Board on which it could and did form the opinion that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of M/s Barium Chemical Ltd. is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons, or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive of any of its members, or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or illegal purpose; and (iv) that he had seen the papers and agreed with his two Under Secretaries and the Regional Director that a "deeper probe" was necessary ' There is no hint even in this affidavit that the circumstances were such as to suggest fraud, intent to cheat or misconduct.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to five years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . On appeal, the High Court drew from this conclusion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and convicted them accordingly under section 411 I.P.C., and sentenced them to 5 years ' R.I. and fine. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, According to him there is no other evidence in the present case which points to the complicity of the 14 appellants in the crime of dacoity and therefore as they cannot be suspected to be dacoits themselves, the only presumption to be drawn is one of receivers of stolen property or as receivers of property which was stolen in a dacoity. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against him. It is only when the accused cannot be connected with the Crime except by reason of possession of the fruits of crime that the rule may be drawn. [723 H] In the present ease, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods were found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders and they have been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. It may be that these 20 persons were merely receivers of theft property from some other 20 persons who are the dacoits.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to Government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio additional law secretary to the government in law Department, member administrative tribunal and the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, in all 15 in number. All these officers are the members of the service of the State and they were before 1962 presiding over district courts or courts subordinate to them and as such were under the control of the High Court. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the Registrar is exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Courts as such nor the Governor has any hand in his appointment. The power to transfer a district judge from one post to another whether as a Judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands. It appears that for some time past there were differences between the High court and the Government about the posting of some judicial officers. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of these administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The Government by its letter of April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to adhere to the principle of three years service in an appointment at a particular station against a special post. But when it came to the question of implementing that policy, the Government was reluctant. Every time the High ' Court requested the government to release the three officers mentioned above for being posted as district and Session judges or addl. district and session judges as the case may be, the government turned down those requests on one ground or the other.

Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 as it originally stood underwent substantial changes in 1960 and as amended read as under: "15. Persons in whom right of pre emption vests in respect of sales of agricultural land and village immovable property shall vest (a) where the sale is by a female of land or property to which she has succeeded through her father or brother 's son, or daughter 's sons of the vendor or vendors; (b) where such sale is of a share out of joint land or properties and is not made by all the co sharers jointly, only the other co shar ers and the tenants can exercise the right of preemption. " The right of Pre ememption based on consanguinity was upheld on the consideration that if an outsider is introduced as a co sharer in a property it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. The right conferred by section 15(i)(a), clauses 'fourthly ' and 'thirdly ' of section 15 (1)(b) and clause fourthly of section15(1) (c) as valid and not infringing Articles 14 or 15 of the Constitution. This Court, however, did not find any justification for the classification contained in section 15 which conferred a right on co shar er to pre empt, the confer ment of that right on certain kinsfolk based on the rule of consangubility being a relic of the feudal past totally inconsistent with the constitutional philosophy and scheme. It also found the list of kins folk entitled to preempt as a sub sharer i.e. father 's broth er 's father ' broth ing ' son of the vendors in male line in order of succession; secondly, in the co divideders, if any, who are agnates, in order, of succession and thirdly, in persons not included under firstly or second above, in Order of succession, who but for such sale would be entitled to inherit the properly in the event of his or their decease, in case the son has inherited the land or the property sold from his lather, the right to pre im emption was vested, first in the sons or daughters or son 's daughter 'S son or daughter"s sons or daughter`s sons. This view was upheld by this Court in Atam Prakash vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , and held that what was said about the right was that while co sharors were entitled to Pre empt the conferment of that fight on certain Kinsfilk based upon the rule Of consangu unity being a pre existing past totally consistent with the Constitutional philosophy and Scheme. It further held that in the case of sale of agricultural lands and village immoveable property by a sole owner, the tenant alone can exercise his right of post emption.

The workmen of the appellant company were not entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a, spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sick sickness for which sickness benefit was last paid. The Company applied for and obtained special leave to appeal as aforesaid, with the further direction that the appeal may be heard along with the identical matter (in the Alembic Glass Industries case) and that it would be automatically discon tinued when the benefits of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme would become available to the workmen, and also that the reasonableness of the demand could not be examined by the Tribunal. On behalf of the workmen it was contended that as the benefits under sections 47 and 49 of the Act are already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, and they are quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of the benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribu nal. [83B] 2.1 In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the ground of sickness. [86C] 2:2 In providing that a person qualified to claim sickness benefit shall not be entitled to it for the initial waiting period of two days except in tho case of continuous illness of the nature mentioned therein, "With regard to sick leave, the argument on behalf of appellant was that benefits were granted by the , but that is not a bar to the demand of the workman for sick Leave. The reason is that the first proviso to section 49 of ' the Employees State Insurance Act does not cover all contingencies of sickness and in any event the first three waiting days are not covered. In view of the provisions of the , no provision need be made about sickness leave at all. That this Act has been applied, to the company and that the workmen of tile Company get the benefit of sick leave. [87D E] 2 :3 The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in its view that the workman are entitled to 7 days ' sick leave with wages on full emoluments for a period of seven days when he is certified by a competent medical officer to be ill for that or a longer period. Sickness is a serious misfortune to a workman for it not only prevents him from earning his normal wages but is a drain on his meagre financial resources by way of additional expenditure on food, nursing and visits to the medical centre etc. It has not been disputed before us that the "region cure industry" basis is suitable in cases like the present for examining any controversy regarding the work man 's demands for additional benefits, but it has been argued by the learned counsel for the appel lants that the award of the benefit should not be admissible on the grounds that it had not been allowed by other companies in the region. [88E F] 3:4 The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit to the workman of 7 days sick leave in a year to its employ ees in Bangalore and it is permissible to accumulate it upto 12 days in addition to the current year 's leave, under a settlement dated July 17, 1969 which is being continued even after the coming into force of the . [88F G] 4:5 The benefit of sickness leave was therefore lost when the Act was made applicable to the region from December 15, 1969.

An order of detention passed by the Government of Bombay on the 8th June, 1955, against the appellant before us, who was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay having a standing of about thirty years, was challenged under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that it was passed for ulterior purpose of preventing his freedom of speech and freedom of professional activity in the sphere of Goan affairs by reason of his known views in this behalf. Held: (i) The order of the detention was mala fide as it was made without any real application of mind by the detaining authority, that the authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan National Movement, and that the Police procured the detention order for the purpose of suppressing the freedom of the appellant to ventilate his point of view on the Goon politics and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos. (ii) The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22(6), whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. It follows that both the obligation to furnish particulars and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interests, are vested in the detaining Authority, not in any other manner. (iii) The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue, feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well be implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicated cannot be implied In these circumstances it is unnecessary, therefore, to deal with this case with a theoretical contention as to whether or not article 22 (6) of the constitution overrides the constitutional right to be afforded a reasonable opportunity to make a representation to the Board.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer, Rao assisted her in going away from her parents ' protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He was charged with offences under section 120B I.P.C. and section 161 I. P.C., read with sections 34 to 70 in Ch. VI of which section 45 is as follows : " Any officer, junior commissioned officer or warrant officer who behaves in a manner unbecoming his position and the character expected of him shall, on conviction by court martial, if he is an officer, be liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned". The respondent was called upon to submit his explanation by way of defence regarding the allegations against him. The explanation of Rao was placed before the Central Government. The Central Government found it to be unsatisfactory and on April 9, 1959 an order was passed removing the respondent from service. Rao thereupon filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground inter alia that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Govern ment has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The words "Subject to the provision of this act" occurring therein in section19 make section 19(2)(a) specifically gives power to make a rule providing for the removal from the serv ice of persons subject to the Act. It follows that there may be a valid rule where under, subject to other provisions of the Act, the Central government may remove a man from the Service. Rule 14 is such a rule : it is therefore not ultra vires. [450 C] (2) The two sections 19 and 45 of the , are mutually exclusive. The result is that r .14 of the army Rules, 1955, is not ultra rites the .

Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down sec. 28 only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an unguided, uncanalised and uncanalalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that sec.28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The policy and the Scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. In fact, sec. 5(1) requires that the Administrator should have regard to the policy and purposes of the .Act in making his orders. Moreover against his order under that Sec a revision lies to Central Government which implies that he will have to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec . Moreover, regard must be had to be the nature of the restrictions imposed by the section. [955C D] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division while declaring unamended sec. 27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague.

The properties involved in the suit consist of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli district. According to the appellants, the said lands had been granted in Inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavaravar Temple by the Carnatic Rulers before the advent of British power in India. The original grant deeds were not available; but at the time of settlement of the Inams in sixties of the last century, Inam title deeds were issued in favour of the family of Pachathai Kandi Udayaravar Temple at Eravudi village. The appellants averred that the properties covered by the grant bad been granted to the original grantee burdened with the obligation of performing certain services in a Matam; and that the said properties had been alienated from time to time, and as a result of the first alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. The trial Judge examined the whole evidence and came to the conclusion that the grant of the Inam was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour Of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the lower appellate Court reversed the finding of the lower Appellate Court that the existence of the temple had not been proved; but held that the appellants had proved their title to the suit properties. The High Court also took the view that the question as to whether on facts proved in this case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of a temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that article 134 B would not apply to the present case because the alienations evidenced by Exts. A 3, A 6 and A 12 show that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of any temple but in their individual character as owners of the said property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether a transfer effected by the manager of a Hindu religious endowment on the basis that it belongs to him and not to the religious endowments, is irrelevant for the purpose of article 134B if it is shown to have been made on the foundation that the transferor treated the properties as his own, it does appear that the two earlier Privy Council decisions in Gnanasambanda 's case lend some support to the contention. (2) The character of the representations made by the previous managers in regard to their relation with the property which is the subject matter of transfer, is relevant for the purposes of article134 B.

Clause 2 of the agreement recites that the licensee had agreed to use the premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the appellant would be entitled to keep the keys of the said shop with him and shall be at liberty to work in the said Premises for twenty hours subject to restriction of rules and regulations imposed by the Municipal or any other local authority or authorities. The licensor had agreed that if he commits any default of any terms and conditions or fails to pay the compensation for two months or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy, the licensor shall be entitled 'to terminate the agreement and cancel and revoke the leave and license granted earlier and shall he entitled to take possession forthwith of the premises. It was further stipulated that the licence would be liable to be cancelled on the licensee surrendering possession of the demised premises by removing himself and his belongings on the expiry of the period for which the agreement or sooner termination or determination thereof after deducting all the dues if any for payment of compensation. The appellant filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he was not a sub tenant as such or not, but only the subtenancy as such and therefore it was recorded that as agreed 'B.C. no preliminary issue was to be framed. The trial Judge in the instant case passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st of January, 1975. [1060C E] 1.2 In determining whether an agreement creates between the parties, the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. & Ors. vs Shri Vishwa Nath & 5 others, [1987] 2 Scale 27, held inapplicable.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of the erstwhile Dholpur Union into the Matsya Union. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former Rajasthan State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. It was also the practice in that State that when permits for export were issued, export duties had to be paid in advance though the actual export was made later. Consequently, in June 1947, the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni, and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. This permit had been granted on June 28, 1947 and remained in force upto December 2, 1947. Thereafter he could not export further as his permit was not extended. He could only export 4,572 maunds and 20 seers of chiuni before December 2. On May 15, 1949, the United State of Rajasthan was formed including the Matsaya Union into which the former State of Dholpur came to be merged in 1949 never recognised the obligations of the latter State unless it chose to recognise the obligation. The respondent 's case further was that though he asked the State for refund of this advance duty, the State did not pay back the same to him. In the meantime, rapid constitutional changes took place after August 15, 1947, by which all the old laws continued till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merging State if there was any liability on the merged State. The suits were resisted by the State of Madhya Pradesh on various grounds; but the High Court dismissed them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be taken to have recognised the rights of the subjects and undertaken the liability, if any, of the old States. It follows therefore that the State would be liable under article 295(2) of the Constitution to meet the liabilities of all old States which eventually were included in it subject always to this that if the new State passed any law repealing the old law which would affect the liability or even otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force. (ii) The expression "Government of the corresponding Indian State" used in article 295 (2) would mean only the United state of Rajasthan as it was just before January 26, 1950 but also the old old laws which came to he merged into it through the process to which we have already referred.

Section 3 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act (Mad XX of 1933) provides that no person shall, within a notified area, set up, establish or use, or continue or allow to be continued any place for the purchase or sale of a notified commercial crop except under and in accordance with the conditions of a licence granted to him by the Collector. The first proviso authorises the State Government to exempt from the provisions of the said sub section any person who carries on the business of purchasing or selling any commercial crop in quantities not exceeding those prescribed by Rules made under the Act. The second proviso enables the Market Committee to exempt a person selling commercial crop which has been grown by him, or a cooperative society registered or deemed to be registered under the Madras Co operative Societies Act, 1932, selling a commercial crop, which has already been grown and opened by the marketing committees within a reasonable radius from the market as may from time to time be fixed by the State Govt. and that nothing under the said Act prevents the Government from fixing a long distance as a prohibited area; with the result that a person, who is having a licence to trade in and about the place where the market is fixed, is deprived of his livelihood which is an unreasonable restriction upon his right to do business unless it is clearly established that the provisions are too drastic, unnecessarily harsh and overreach the scope of the object to achieve which it is enacted. The Act was passed to provide for better regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops by providing suitable and regulated markets by eliminating middlemen and bringing face to face the producer and the buyer so that they may meet on equal terms, thereby eradicating or at any rate reducing the scope for exploitation in dealings. Such a statute cannot be said to create unreasonable restrictions on the citizens ' right to trade unless it was clearly established, that the provision is too drastic and unnecessarily harsh, overreached the scope and purpose of the enactment and defeat its object. It is therefore necessary to scrutinise the provisions Of the Act and the Rules made thereunder to ascertain whether the restrictions imposed are not reasonable. Under section 3, the State Govern ment issues a notification declaring their intention to exercise control over the purchase and sale of such commercial crop or crops in a particular area and calling for objections and suggestions to be made within a prescribed time. After the objections are received, the Government considers them and declares the areas to be specified in the notification or any portion thereof to be a notified Area for the purpose of this Act in respect of commercial crop and crops specified in that notification. Under sub section (4) a person is exempted from the operation of that rule in respect Of any notified commercial crops grown by himself. The appellants challenged the validity of the provisions on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that they were running the market at as an occupation or business with high standards and that the notification directing the constitution of a Market Committee in the same locality, when admittedly the entire scheme of building a net work of markets could not be finished within a predictable time, was not a reasonable restriction on their right to carry on trade or business; (2) that the appellants had really two fundamental rights: one is to carry out trade or 'business and the other is to hold their property, i.e., the market; that by reason of the notification they were not prevented from doing their business, for they could still do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also do business outside the prescribed area ; and (3) that under both the sub clauses they were entitled to do under that section, but made the bye law mentioning the mahimai ' allowance as one not deductible in any transaction.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed their conviction on the ground that the sentence in each case should be commuted to transportation for life. Held, (per curiam) that a common intention presupposes prior concert and arrangement can, and indeed often must be determined from subsequent conduct as for example by a systematic plan of campaign unfolding itself during the course of the action which could only be referable to prior concert, and pre arrangement or a running away together in a body or a meeting together subsequently. But when appellate Judges who agree on the question of guilt differ on that of sentence, it is usual not to impose the death penalty unless there are compelling reasons. In the present case the facts disclosed did not warrant an inference of common intention even if one had been charged. There was no evidence of any prior meeting which could justify the conclusion of a common object even if two Judges concur because of section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and it was for that reason that they must have joined in the attack and so have added that detail to their story. It was not enough, as in the latter Privy Council case, to have the same intention independently of each other, e.g., the intention to rescue another and, if necessary, to kill those who oppose. In a case like that, each would be individually liable for whatever injury he caused but none could be vicariously convicted for the act of any of the others; and if the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he cannot be convicted of the murder however clearly an intention to kill could be proved in his case. Barendra Kumar Ghosh vs King Emperor, (1945) L.R. 52 I.A. 45, followed.

There was medical examination by the doctor on the life of the deceased on 27st December,1960 and it was further alleged that the payment of the first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal and advised the deceased to pay the first premiums in full. It was also stated that the said two cheques were encashed and the appellant had duly appropriated the amount and credited in the accounts towards the premium payable by the deceased. The Divisional Manager, Masulpatam Branch, denied liability on behalf of the appellant Corporation on 28th January 1961. Thereafter there was correspondence between the parties between 1st February, 1961 to 23rd December, 1963 wherein the respondents plaintiffs had claimed the payment and the appellants had denied liability for the same. On the 10th of January,1964, the respondents filed the suit in which it was alleged that there was a concluded and valid insurance contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January. 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. The Trial Court held that there is no concluded contract between them and the corporation, was untenable, according to the plaintiffs. It further noted that it was significant that the case set out in the plaint and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to the Corporation was not that the proposal was as a matter of fact accepted by the Divisional Manager on the other hand, claim was that it should be deemed to have been accepted. Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the price at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili tities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at the factory gate was Rs.5, then in such a case the value would be Rs.30 being the value of the grey cloth plus the value for the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses. That would be the correct as sessable value. If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the operator as to what would be his price at what he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable value of processed fabric and excise duty would be charged to the farce on that basis provided that the declaration as to the prices at which he would he selling the processing goods in a market, would include only the price or deemed price at that which the processed fabric would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. It is necessary to include the processor"s expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to mention the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math, Sauna temple and that Mahant Sadashiva Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar. It was claimed that in the event of Mahant Sadasiva Yatati being found out of possession a decree for possession should be made. Sadashiv Yati pleaded that on the death of Mahant Shivshanker Yati he was elected Mahant of Math Saa and was, therefore, entitled as Sarbarkar to all the properties recorded in the deity Mahadeo Ji or in the name of Mahant Sri Shivshankar Yati. The suit was contested by the first defendant, Kedar Nath, also referred to as Uma Shankar Yati, who had formerly been married men and householders, men who had passed through the grihastha ashram. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashv yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of the Math and Sarbbarakar of the deity. Both appeals were filed in the High Court. First Appeal No. 80 of 1964 was filed by Kedar Nath for the relief that Sadasiv Yatti being found Out of possession, a decree should be passed. The other appeal, First Appeal NO. 270 of 1965 was filed against the declaration that the Amauli properties were owned by the Math or the deity and that SadhatashivYati was a properly constituted Mahant. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. It held that the income from the properties belonging to the math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog arpan, arpan deepdan daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed. The present appeal is directed against that part of the judgment and order of the High court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. There can be no presumption either way. All the facts and circumstances must be taken into consideration and on a balancing of the entire evidence it has to be determined whether the property can be said to belong to the Mahant or deity or is the personal property of the Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. Their father Sardar Nand Singh who was 42 330 found entitled to quasi permanent allotments of 40 standard acres, and 5 1/4 unit of land was given quasipermanent allotment in another village named Humbran in the same district. The two villages were, however, 25 miles or so distant from each other. Nand Singh made an application for consolidation of his lands with those of the appellants in the Village Raikot. During the pendency of this application he died and after his death, the application was continued by the appellants. This application was rejected on the ground that no land was available in the villages Raikot and that consequently their allotment had been wrongly made but referred the matter back to the Additional Custodian for decision. The appellants then moved the Deputy Custodian General for calling up their review application and for revising the order of October 31, 1952 passed by the Additional Deputy Custodian cancelling the allotment of land in favour of the 14 allottees which had originally been cancelled earlier. As a result of this order the allotment made in favour Of the appellants automatically stood cancelled. On January 6, 1955, the appellants moved the Assistant Custodian General who dismissed the application on the view that r. 14(6) of the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour 'of the appellants by the order dated October 31. 1952. On December 17, 1954 the appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General which was dismissed on August 20, 1952. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the power of the Custodian under the , to deal with matters of this kind had been taken away by virtue of the provisions of section 12(2) and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. Held: (i) The powers conferred by sub section (1) of section 19 of the Act are confined only to properties which are entrusted to them for management and not with respect to any other property. Section 17 deals with the function; and duties of managing officers and managing corporations. Sub section (2) provides that subject to the provisions Of the Act and the rules made thereunder, a managing officer or a managing corporation may, among other things, take such measures as he or it considers necessary or expedient for the purpose of securing, administering, preserving, managing or disposing of any property in the compensation pool entrusted to him or it. etc.

In the elections held to the Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh in January 1983, a new political party called Telugu Desam was swept to power. It assumed office on January 9, 1983. On February 8, 1983 an order (G.O. Ms. No. 36) was issued by the Government of Andhra pradesh stating that it had decided to reduce the age of superannuation of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service from 58 to 58 years. Two notifications issued in exercise of the power conferred by the Proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution were appended to that order. The Fundamental Rules were amended by the first notification, while the corresponding rules of the Hyderabad Civil Services Rules were amend ed by the second notification. By these notifications, every Government servant, whether ministerial or non ministerial but not belonging to the last grade Service, who had already attained the age Of 55 years was to retire from service with effect from February 28, 1983, on the ground that it has become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths. Over 18,000 government employees and 10,000 public sector employees were superannuated as a result of the order. In 1979, when the first order was issued, the impugned law gave to the employees a notice of 20 days only since all such employees had to retire on February 28. 1983. The petitioners challenged the Ordinance on the grounds: (a) that there was no basis at all for reducing the age by fixing the age; and (b) that it is arbitrary, irrational and unconnected with the object which it seeks to achieve. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1. It is well settled that the service rules can be as much amended, as they can be made, under the proviso to Article 311 read with article 313 and that, the power to amend these rules carries with it the power of amending them retrospectively. Therefore, the amendment made to the Fundamental Rules in the exercise of powers conferred by Article 309, by which the proviso was deleted retrospectively, was a valid exercise of legislative power. [604C D] 1.2. The amendment made in the Fundamental Rule was beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature. By that amendment, a proviso was added to rule 2 which reads thus: "Provided that the rules shall not be modified or E; replaced to the disadvantage of any person already in service." By G.O.(Ms. No 36) the Government decided on its own to increase the age from 55 to 58. The specific case of the State Government on the question of reduction of the age was stated thus: (1) that the recommendation made by the Pay Commission was casual and was not based on relevant criteria; and that as many as 1204,008 educated youths were left without employment on September 30, 1979 as a consequence of the unwarranted increase in the age.
