Explanation 6 inserted in section 2(p) read with the provisoes inserted in s.24(1) w.e.f. 31.3.1983 and their amendment in 1986 have also a bearing in the cases of raw materials purchased for manufacture of guar gum and utensils where the purchase is exempt even if purchased by a registered dealer for the purpose of export within the State or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than through way of sales in the State, or despatching them to a places outside the state in any such manner as may be prescribed.

The appellants were registered dealers under the Bombay Sales Tax Act. In their return of turnover for the period from April 1, 1954 to March 31, 1955 they claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of sales of cotton of the total value of Rs. 68,493 2 6 and sales of castor oil on the ground that these sales were oil FOB contracts under which they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and so no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b). The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption and assessed them to sales tax on a taxable turnover including these sales. He also assessed them as to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Act on their purchase of cast or oil which they later sold for the sum of Rs 6,47,509 1 6 as mentioned above. The notice of demand for the total sales tax and the purchase tax assessed was served on the sellers on September 30, 1956. The sellers thereupon moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of assessment and the notice of the demand and for prohibiting the Sales Tax officer from taking any steps pursuant to the order or the notice. The learned Judge who heard the petition rejected the sellers ' contention that the goods remained their property till these crossed the Customs frontier and therefore held that the sellers were not entitled to the benefit of article 285(1) (b). As regards the assessment to purchase Tax also he rejected the seller 's contention that they remained their properties till the time these crossed customs barrier. The High Court dismissed the application under article 227 of the Constitu tion. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants dealers that the word " a person" instead of the words " a registered dealer " is deliberate and that it was the intention of the Legislature to levy purchase tax on goods specified in column I of Schedule B, at the rates, if any, specified against such goods in column 4 of the said schedule, "where a certificate under cl. (b) is furnished in respect Of such goods and the purchasing dealer does not show to the satisfaction of the Collector that the Goods have been despatched by him or by a person to whom he has sold the goods to an address outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by the dealer furnishing such certificate ".

The respondent husband married the appellant (wife) as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later had a son by her. 15 The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted, marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat, in Bombay, to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a reference to mehar money (Rs. 5,000/ and Rs. 180/ ) which was also stated to have been adjusted by the compromise terms. There were a clause in the compromise that the appellant declares that she had now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the respondent was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs 400/ for her subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the Respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband who on a strange view of the law that the court under section 125 had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The High Court dismissed the revision petition and summarily dismissed a revision petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code which provides that "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from, her husband and has not remarried. On this foundation he urged that accepting the contention of the respondent that the wife was a divorcee his client was still entitled to an allowance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Every divorce otherwise eligible is entitled to the benefit of maintenance allowance and the dissolution of the marriage makes no difference to this right under the current Code. In the normal course, an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the learned Magistrate at the trial level. However, the husband has not examined himself to prove that he has been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His plea is his right to ignore. So the basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. In a welfare oriented jurisdiction, a broader perception and appreciation of the facts and their bearing must govern the verdict not chopping little logic or tinkering with burden of proof. The next submission is that the absence of mutual consent to live separately must be made out if the hurdle of section 125 (4) is to be over come. [78G H; 79A B] 2.1 Section 127(3)(b) posits the goal and relieves; the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The purpose of the payment 'under any customary or personal law ' must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The whole scheme of section 127(4)(b), is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. Law is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic but purposeful.

The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai Sansthan. Though the origin of the Sansthan is dipped somewhat in antiquity and direct testimony was lacking, it has never been disputed that Sakharam Maharaj constructed a temple in the year 1817 at Amalner and installed the aforesaid deity according to religious rites. He also acquired certain properties and the said temple with the properties constituted Shri Vithalrao Deshmukh of Amalerner. The sansthan had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the values of Rs, 1,06,000/ and the average gross annual income as well as the average annual expenditure was Rs. 11,000 / . After passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act 1950 (No. 29 of 1950) an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons Bhaskarrao Chimanrao Deshmukh, Ramrao Sahebrao Deshmukh and Ramkrishna Tryambak Deshpande, as constituted attorneys of Vasudeobuwa who was described in the application as the "owner" of the property. The word 'Buwa means saint. The application was made on May 29, 1952 to the Assistant Charity Commissioner, Poona under protest and without prejudice to the claim made therein that the Sansthan was not a public trust. In view of the penal provision under section 66 of the Act in the case of non compliance with section 18(1) of the said Act, the said application was filed ex abundanti cautela. The Assistant Charity Commis sioner after requisite notice made an enquiry into the matter in accordance with the provisions of the . On behalf of the applicants representing the Sansthan evidence of the attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande was recorded and he was cross examined by the assessors as well by the Assistant Commissioner. Some documents were also produced on behalf of them. The District Judge reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner by his order dated October 16, 1959 and declared the Sansthan to be a private property and not a 'public trust '. The High Court set aside the order of the District Judge and restored that of the Deputy Charity Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the applicants: (1) that there is absolutely no evidence in this case about dedication to the public or public user of the temple as a matter of right; (2) that the High Court failed to consider all the material documents filed on behalf by the appellant except exhibit 35 and that the conclusion was highly erroneous being contrary to the one that had been reached by the District judge on appraisal of the entire documentary evidence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) It is not always possible to have all the features of a public Trust in a given case. Even some of the tests laid down by this Court may be sufficient to enable the court to come to a conclusion about the character of the trust on documentary evidence, if any, the object and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner in Which the property had long been used by the public, the contribution of the public to all intents and purposes, as a matters of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the state of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the endowment, the nature of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a 'private or a public religious endowment. [521 C E] (ii) It has been held that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol it is a private and not as a public endowment, as the persons who are entitled to worship at the shrine of the deity can only be the members of the family, and that is an ascertained group of individuals.

The appellants are the trustees of a Port Trust Employees ' Union. The respondents to this appeal are the Trustees of the Port of Bombay. The dispute in the present case was whether the existing system of work of shore crew of the Prince 's and Victoria Docks under which each shift system consisted of 8 hours ' normal duty, 2 hours ' variable recess and 12 hours ' overtime needs any modification? The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing systems of work needed any modification. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that section 13 fixes the number of hours constituting a normal working day for an adult can be so arranged that inclusive of intervals for rest it shall not spread over more than 12 hours on any day; and (2) that in some employments time for work depends on some 643 extraneous factors and hours of rest cannot always be fixed to, break up those hours. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) On a single day the number Of hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours of ' rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. It is wrong to contend that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest. In a 12 hour shift, the nine hours of worked on any one day can be spread over 12 hours and the extra hours will necessarily be hours of part of the normal workingday which may also include one or more specified intervals. [637 B C] (ii) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal Working day is achieved by pres cribing that the hours Of work in a six day week shall not exceed 48, although on any particular day the hours are of rest, provided the period is specified beforehand, and the workman is neither called upon to work nor expected to work. Having thus distinguished between periods of work, and interval of rest it makes up their 9 hours which is 8 hours work and one hour interval for rest. They are, therefore, entitled to three hours ' wages overtime if required to work beyond the 9 hours on a day. [643 D E] (iii) The workmen compared the case of the Union that in the former there was 3 hours ' adolescent recess is in force at the Prince "s and James Docks work in different way and their case cannot be compared with that of the Flotilla Crew or the crew crew at the Alexandra Docks.

The trial court decreed the suit holding that at the time when the appeal of the respondent was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of thika tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a consideration of the provisions of the Act and the Ordinance, the Subordinate judge held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice of quit in accordance with section 3 as he was a thikatenant within the meaning of the said Act as it was finally amended. The decree holder put the decree in execution and recovered possession of the land on December 18, 1949. The appeal filed therefrom by the second defendant was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court by certificate, HELD: (1) The benefit of section 28 was available only if the decree or order for the recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of the Calcutta Thika Amendment Act, 1952, but possession of such holding had not been recovered from him. If any such pending suit or proceeding related to any matter in respect of which the Controller was competent to pass orders, the suit or proceedings would be transferred to the controller who would deal with it in accordance With the provisions Of the Act just as if the Act had been in operation on the date when the commencement of that Act; but he was to deal with all pre Act suits on the basis that no notice under section 4 was necessary. [176 E F] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. (2) The language of sections 4 and 5 leaves no room for doubt that after the coming into force of the , it was not open to the landlord either to allege any of the grounds specified in section 3 or to prove the existence thereof at the hearing of the suit, he had to establish the existence of such a ground when the suit is heard. All that the section lays down is that ejectment could not be had unless the existence Of one of the ground was proved. As section 4 of the 1949 Act was prospective only, it could not apply to this case. [177 D E] Mahaddeol Mal Kanodia & Anr. vs AdministratorGeneral of WestBengal, ; and MahadeonolalKanodia vs administrator General ofWest Bengal, , referred to. (3) The word 'successor in interest ' had not not been defined in the Act or in the Ordinance but as words in the statute were under section 2 sub section (6) to have the same meaning as those used in the and the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 it would, but for the amendment of the definition Of a thka tenant, have meant only those persons who inherited from tenants and not those who acquired by purchase.

Prior to 1965, in the High Court of Allahabad Bench Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs 120 300 to Section officers. In 1965, the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference. The Committee was asked to consider the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. It was also required to recommend as far as possible equal emoluments for identical duties and responsibility. The State Government accepted the recommendations. Subsequently, these pay scales were raised to Rs. 200 450 and Rs.515 715 respectively. Being dissatisfied with the down grading, the Bench Secretaries made representation to the Government. They demanded that they should at least be put at par with Section Officers if not on higher scale. The High Court upheld their claim but half heartedly. Aggrieved by the decision of the High court, the Union of India appealed to this Court. On behalf of the respondents it was contended: (1) In comparison to Bench Secretaries, the section officers of the secretariat have to bear more responsibilities in their Section and have to control over its subordinates; (2) The pay scale recommended by the Pay Commission need not have any amendments; (3) It should be appropriate for the Bench Secre taries to accept promotional posts in the Pay scale ofRs.500 1,000 as recommended by Pay Commission. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (i) In contrast to Bench Secretary Grade I, there can be and there are different grades in a service, with varying qualification for entry into a particular grade, the higher grade often being a promotional avenue for officers of tho lower grade. The higher qualifications for the higher post, which may be either academic qualifications or experience based on length of service reasonably sustain the classification of the officers into two grades with different scales of pay. The principle of equal pay for equal work would be an abstract doctrine not attracting Article 14 if sought to be applied to them. It is well known that there can he and there were different grades In a service with varying qualifications for entry in a particular Grade, the lower grade often having being a promotion for those who come directly from Lower Division Assistants and a third promotion for these persons who are promoted first to Upper Division Assistant and then a Bench Secretary. The work of the Bench Secretary is of a great importance. It would be detrimental to the interest of the service itself. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of Pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal payfor equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution. But it follows naturally that equal Pay for unequal work will be a negation of that right. And said: "The same amount of physical work may entail different quality of work, some more sensitive. Some requiring more tact, some less it varies from nature and culture of employment.

The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was for a periods exceeding one year it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. On September 21, 1955, the Raja issued a notice calling upon the appellant to show cause within two months from the date of receipt of that notice as to why the lease should not be terminated without any compensation under the second Proviso to section20(1). The writ petition having come up for hearing before Umamaheswaram, J., on July 18, 1955 made an order directing the Government to hold an enquiry under section 20 of the Madras Estate (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 and decide whether the lease had been given prior or subsequent to that date.
